result: The study established a collection of 58 NMEC isolates from seven geographic regions spanning 1974-2020, with the majority (88%) from high-income countries in Europe, Australia, and North America, and 12% from Cambodia. The authors acknowledge this geographic limitation as a reflection of the difficulty in acquiring isolates causing this disease.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly noted that the collection includes isolates from 'just seven countries' with the majority from high-income countries, stating 'it is not clear how well the results reflect the global diversity of NMEC, nor the populations of NMEC affecting the most populous regions.' This directly challenges the generalizability of the findings despite acknowledging the collection's value.

result: The NMEC isolates showed phylogenetic diversity spanning phylogroups A, B2, C, D, and F, with the majority (82.8%) belonging to phylogroup B2. The isolates belonged to 22 different sequence types, with ST95 (34.5%) and ST1193 (15.5%) being the two most common. ST95 isolates were obtained throughout the entire study period (1974-2020), while ST1193 isolates were only obtained from 2013 onwards.
evaluation: Reviewers described the 'population genomic analyses are comprehensive' and noted the study 'characterising the genomic features of E. coli isolated from neonatal meningitis.' The phylogenetic and sequence type findings are presented as solid data without specific critique.

result: The high incidence of NM associated with ST95 and ST1193 does not reflect the broader prevalence of major ExPEC clones in the Enterobase database, suggesting these lineages exhibit specific virulence features associated with their capacity to cause NM. The authors speculate this is due to the K1 polysialic acid capsule in combination with other virulence factors and the immature immune system of preterm infants.
evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the genomic analyses are 'solid' and 'comprehensive,' the interpretation about specific virulence features is presented as speculation and inference by the authors. Reviewers noted a weakness: 'without knowing their frequency in the broader E. coli population it is hard to know the significance' of the virulence factors, which directly relates to this interpretive claim.

result: The study identified prevalent virulence genes in NMEC including iron uptake systems (enterobactin 98%, yersiniabactin 98%, aerobactin 62%, salmochelin 55%), heme receptors (chuA 93%, hma 62%), adhesins (type 1 fimbriae 100%, mat fimbriae 98%, fdeC 98%), and toxins (usp 83%). No single virulence gene profile was conserved in all isolates, but genes encoding fimbrial adhesins, iron acquisition systems, the K1 capsule, and O antigen types O18, O75, and O2 were most prevalent.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly noted a weakness: 'The virulence factors section highlights several potentially interesting genes that are present at apparently high frequency in the NMEC genomes; however without knowing their frequency in the broader E. coli population it is hard to know the significance of this.' This indicates the data are presented but their interpretation and significance remain uncertain without comparative context.

result: Direct comparison revealed that ST95 isolates contained significantly more virulence factors than ST1193 isolates (p<0.001, Mann-Whitney two-tailed unpaired test).
evaluation: This statistical comparison is presented with clear methodology and p-value. Reviewers described the 'genomic analyses are high quality' and 'population genomic analyses are comprehensive,' which encompasses this type of comparative analysis. No specific critique was raised about this finding.

result: K1 was the dominant capsule type (74.1%), confirmed by ELISA in all but two of 34 tested isolates. O18 was the most common O antigen (27.6%), followed by O75 (13.9%) and O2 (12.1%). H7 was the most dominant H antigen (32.8%), followed by H5 (22.4%) and H4 (15.5%). The most common serotype was O18:H7:K1 (24.1%), belonging to ST95 clonal complex.
evaluation: Reviewers stated the 'genomic analyses are high quality' and 'comprehensive.' The serotyping data are presented with experimental validation (ELISA) and no specific concerns were raised about these findings.

result: ST1193 isolates contained fluoroquinolone resistance mutations (gyrA S83L D87N, parC S80I), and 77.8% harbored genes conferring resistance to aminoglycosides, trimethoprim, and sulphonamides. Six of seven Cambodian isolates had multiple antibiotic resistance genes, with CAM-NMEC-6 containing 14 resistance genes including resistance to third-generation cephalosporins and carbapenems. Overall, antibiotic resistance genes occurred infrequently in the collection.
evaluation: Reviewers described the 'genomic analyses are high quality' without raising specific concerns about the antibiotic resistance findings. The data are presented with clear genomic evidence and regional context.

result: Three patients suffered recrudescent invasive NMEC infection during 2019-2020. In all cases, the infecting isolates were susceptible to therapy (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone), and whole-genome sequencing demonstrated that the isolate causing recrudescence was the same as the original causative isolate. Patient 1's isolates were identical ST1193 with no SNPs. Patient 2's isolates were ST537 with one SNP in mdoH in the blood isolate. Patient 3's isolates were identical ST131.
evaluation: Reviewers stated the 'case study investigations are convincing' and noted the study 'documents bacterial persistence and reinfection in two case studies.' The whole-genome sequencing data demonstrating strain identity across infection episodes are presented as solid evidence without critique.

result: The causative E. coli isolate was detected in Patient 2's fecal sample at the time of recrudescent infection (day 77), suggesting NMEC can persist in the gut and cause repeat infection. Metagenomic sequencing revealed severe gut dysbiosis in patients with recrudescent infection, and the infecting isolate was detected in the intestinal microflora. The authors conclude that even when appropriate antibiotics are used, they may not eliminate the causative NMEC residing intestinally, creating a refractory reservoir that may seed recrudescent infection.
evaluation: Reviewers stated 'In two cases they also found evidence for gut persistence of the NMEC strain, which may act as a reservoir for persistence and reinfection in neonates. This finding is of clinical importance as it suggests that decolonisation of the gut could be helpful in preventing relapse of meningitis in NMEC patients.' The case study investigations were described as 'convincing,' indicating reviewer acceptance of this key finding.

result: Patient 3's microbiome was dominated by Enterococcus (93% and 97.4% relative abundance) at both timepoints examined. E. coli was not detected by fimH amplicon sequencing and had extremely low relative abundance (<0.01%) in fecal samples. The extensive dysbiosis is likely an outcome of three rounds of antibiotic treatment.
evaluation: This is presented as part of the case study data on gut dysbiosis and persistence. Reviewers found the 'case study investigations are convincing' without raising specific concerns about the microbiome findings for Patient 3.

result: Eighteen NMEC isolates were completely sequenced using Oxford Nanopore Technology, representing 11 different sequence types. This work more than tripled the number of available NMEC genomes that can be used as references in future studies.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly stated 'The study presents complete genome sequences for n=18 diverse isolates, which will serve as useful references for future studies of NMEC.' This is identified as a strength of the study.

result: The resistance profile of ST1193 may lead to clinical failure of empiric regimens such as ampicillin and gentamicin used to treat NM and early-onset sepsis. Some ST1193 isolates have been reported to have co-resistance to third-generation cephalosporins, which would limit antibiotic treatment choices.
evaluation: This clinical interpretation is based on the documented resistance genes in ST1193 isolates. Reviewers noted the work 'will be of interest to people involved in the management of neonatal meningitis patients,' suggesting acceptance of the clinical relevance of the resistance findings.

result: The study acknowledges several limitations: lack of complete stool samples spanning pre- and post-treatment, no access to maternal samples (thus cannot rule out mother-to-child transmission as a reinfection mechanism), and missing clinical data on weeks of gestation for all patients.
evaluation: These are limitations explicitly acknowledged by the authors. Reviewers did not dispute these limitations but rather noted them as factors affecting the scope and interpretation of the findings.
